summary: Our project turns NASA nighttime-light imagery and satellite data into synchronized sound and moving map scans. The project includes two visual sonifications: a global 2012–2023 change map, where purple and orange guide pitch and volume, and India-centered annual night-light frames, where pixel brightness and coverage shape the notes. A data-based approach compares quality-screened VIIRS radiance from 2012 and 2023 across selected city regions, mapping spatial changes into chords. The challenge asked us to make the Earth science accessible and we believe that with providing both approaches we have made it engaging and accessible. Our interactive player lets audiences switch between places and years, watch each scan, and understand how the sound is made. By offering an auditory way to explore patterns in Earth-at-night observations, we make NASA data more approachable. It also distinguishes image-based interpretation from numerical radiance comparison. This project is important as it is going to help communities and young adults get a basic idea on sonification, with different major cities and understand how we can map different colors, intensity, radiance changes to sounds.
details:
Our project, NoteBlock, is an interactive way to explore Earth’s nighttime lights through maps and sound. People can choose the global map, an India map from a particular year, or a city map, then watch a synchronized scan while listening. Our website also explains how each map is translated into sound.

We developed two visual approaches and one data-based approach. For the global map, we classify its purple and orange colors and scan across it in sections: purple raises the pitch, orange lowers it, and the amount of classified color affects the volume.

For India, we analyze brightness in NASA’s yearly map images and turn a grid of those brightness patterns into chords. This approach sonifies the image’s brightness; it does not distinguish the map’s “more light” and “less light” colors.

For the city maps, the notebook compares quality-screened VIIRS radiance from 2012 and 2023. The direction and size of the change, along with its position on the grid, shape the sound.

We hope the project makes NASA night-light information more engaging and offers another way to notice patterns across places and years. Its creative element is the set of clear, repeatable rules that connect what people see on the map to what they hear. The player presents those rules alongside each video so listeners can understand the sonification, rather than hearing an unexplained soundtrack.

We used Python notebooks in Google Colab to process the imagery and data, with tools including NumPy, h5py, tifffile, Matplotlib, and FFmpeg. The interactive website uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The project runs on a standard computer and requires no specialized hardware.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, clarity, sound and scan synchronization, and making the interface easy to navigate. We also distinguish image-based sonification from numerical radiance comparison: neither method by itself explains why night lights changed.
